claims.text: As a traditional edo-mae sushi counter, dishes are served with and prepared using soy sauce and nikiri glaze, which contain wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce or accommodation is documented.
The kitchen is entirely fish- and seafood-focused with dashi and fish-based seasonings throughout the omakase course; there is no documented vegan preparation or separation.
The gluten-free 米粉麺 rice noodle is a swap on the standard menu; ramen kitchens boil all noodles in one shared pot, so the rice noodle is cooked in water contaminated by wheat noodles.
No dedicated gluten-free preparation or celiac protocol is claimed anywhere on the shop's own site or listings.
The signature bowls are 醤油らぁ麺 (soy-sauce ramen) and 塩らぁ麺 (salt ramen); Japanese ramen tare of this style is finished with wheat-based soy sauce, and no tamari/gluten-free soy sauce is advertised.
The base broth is a fish-and-pork double soup, so any vegetarian/vegan request would share equipment and stock area with animal broths; no separate vegan line is confirmed.
Ordering is via ticket vending machine with no reservations; no documented allergen handling or celiac accommodation beyond the noodle swap.
Kitchen advertises no added amino-acid seasoning and no hydrolyzed vegetable protein, and a rice-flour noodle can be requested in place of the wheat noodle.

name: 太閤うどん 中町店 (Taiko Udon Nakamachi-ten)

claims.text: The udon noodles are made from a blend of three domestic wheat flours, and tempura uses wheat batter; no gluten-free option is documented.
The standard dashi uses Marushima soy sauce from Shodoshima (a conventional wheat-based shoyu) along with bonito, mackerel and anchovy, so the regular broth is neither vegan nor wheat-free.
For plant-based tempura and fried items, the shop prepares a dedicated oil and pot used only for plant-based items, kept separate from other customers' orders.
Foreign-language menus and a clearly marked vegan menu are available, and the vegan dishes are explicitly stated to contain no animal-derived ingredients.
The vegan dashi is made 100% from plant materials (kombu, vegetables and fruit) after extensive in-house research.
Dedicated separate oil and pot are used for plant-based tempura to avoid cross-contact with animal products.

name: 大衆ぎょうざ倶楽部 餃夢中 広島本通店 (Taishu Gyoza Club Gyomuchu Hiroshima Hondori)

claims.text: Gyoza wrappers are wheat-based and fried/boiled in a shared kitchen; no gluten-free preparation or dedicated equipment is documented.
Dipping sauces and izakaya seasonings are standard soy-sauce-based, which normally contains wheat; no wheat-free alternative is noted.
Core dishes are pork gyoza and fried chicken cooked in shared pans and fryers; no vegan menu or separated preparation is documented.

name: 台湾薬膳料理 青葉 (Taiwan Yakuzen Ryori Aoba)

claims.text: Taiwanese/Chinese cooking here relies on soy-sauce-based seasonings and sauces that are normally wheat-based; no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned.
The signature herbal hot pot broth is animal-based (duck, black-bone chicken, pork meatballs), so vegetable dishes cooked in shared broth or sauces may carry animal content.
With advance notice the kitchen will adjust the herbal hot pot's ingredients to suit a diner's needs, suggesting willingness to customize when asked ahead.
As a tempura specialist, the kitchen fries wheat-battered items throughout; a shared fryer and wheat-based tsuyu make cross-contamination very likely for gluten-free diners.
Dishes and the dipping broth use a dashi/soy-sauce base, which standardly contains wheat.
Menu is built on seafood, eel and fish-based dashi, so vegan diners face pervasive animal-product contact.

name: 貴家。 地蔵通り本店 (Takaya Jizodori Honten)

claims.text: Okonomiyaki is cooked on a shared teppan griddle where wheat batter, wheat noodles, and wheat-containing sauce are all prepared, making cross-contact with gluten effectively unavoidable.
Standard okonomiyaki contains pork, egg, and noodles cooked on a shared griddle alongside other meat dishes; no separate vegan preparation is documented.

name: たけはらの味 ぴぃす (Takehara no Aji Piisu)

claims.text: The signature negi-shabu uses a soy-sauce-based bonito dashi; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the broth and similarly seasoned dishes are not gluten-free.

The cooking is built on a fish (bonito) dashi and the menu is dominated by oysters, sea urchin, pork and beef, so vegan dishes are not available and shared broths/equipment make plant-only meals impractical.
